From her third-floor balcony in the Delhi colony, Deepika saw the crowd forming around a thin man with a clipboard near the park gate.
Her neighbour Bhavna called up, holding her phone. “There's a message! A child-lifter with a clipboard, pretending to do surveys!” The message had a blurry photo that could have been anyone.
Below, twenty people had become forty. Someone grabbed the man's collar. He was shouting, “I'm from the municipal survey!” Nobody listened.
Deepika's hands went cold. She dialled 112 and gave the address, then ran down with her own ID card from work, which looked just like his.
The police van arrived in six minutes and pulled the man into the vehicle, safe. An hour later, the municipal office posted that the survey was real. By then the message had been shared a thousand times.

qa.q: How many minutes did the police van take to arrive?
qa.a: It arrived in six minutes.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling as she watched the crowd grow?
qa.a: Her hands went cold; she felt frightened and alarmed as the rumour turned a crowd against an innocent man.

qa.q: What steps did Deepika take, and why were they wise?
qa.a: She called 112 with the address straight away and went down with an ID card like his, getting protection there without joining the crowd.

qa.q: How might the survey worker have felt when nobody listened?
qa.a: He was likely terrified and helpless, shouting the truth while a crowd grabbed him because of a blurry photo.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a messaging rumour turn a crowd angry at an innocent survey worker, with verified facts arriving late.

“What happened?”
“Someone posted in the market group that he hit a child with his bike and drove off.”
A dozen men had surrounded the rider. One slapped him. He was holding up his hands. “I didn't! I stopped to help!”

She pushed through to a woman holding a crying boy with a scraped knee. “Did the bike hit him?”
“No,” the mother said, startled. “He fell running. That man picked him up.”
Avni shouted it, twice, as loud as she could. The men hesitated. The police jeep arrived five minutes later. By then the rider's lip was bleeding.

Ivan's short video review of a Prague restaurant had gone viral for the wrong reason: he'd mispronounced the chef's name, and people decided he was mocking her. By Sunday there were thousands of comments, some threatening.
His friend Hana didn't post a defence. She messaged him privately: “Hey. Are you reading them?”
“All of them,” Ivan wrote back.
“Stop. Give me your login for an hour. I'll turn off comments and report the threats. Go for a walk. I'll call you at six.”
He hesitated, then sent it.
Hana reported eleven threatening accounts. At six she called. Ivan sounded tired but steadier. “I thought everyone hated me.” “Not everyone,” Hana said. “Not me.”

qa.q: How many threatening accounts did Hana report?
qa.a: Hana reported eleven threatening accounts.

qa.q: How was Ivan feeling when he said everyone hated him?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and ashamed, as if everyone was against him after reading all the comments.

qa.q: Why was Hana's private help more useful than a public defence?
qa.a: She stopped him reading, reported the threats and stayed in touch by phone, which gave him real support without adding to the noise.

qa.q: How might the chef have felt about the viral video?
qa.a: She might have felt mixed, perhaps hurt at first by the mispronunciation, and uneasy about the anger done in her name.

grounding: Shows a friend privately messaging a pile-on target, helping her friend stop reading comments and reporting abuse.
